seo_title: Insurance Appraiser vs Adjuster: Key Differences Explained
meta_description: Insurance appraiser vs adjuster: who each works for, what each decides, and when to hire an independent appraiser in Texas.
h1: Insurance Appraiser vs Adjuster: What's the Real Difference?
excerpt: Adjusters investigate coverage and propose payment; appraisers resolve disputes over the amount of loss. Learn who works for whom and when Texans should hire an appraiser.
key_takeaways: Adjusters decide coverage and propose payment; appraisers decide only the amount of loss.
Staff and independent adjusters work for the insurer; public adjusters work for the policyholder.
Appraisal starts with a written demand under your policy's appraisal clause.
An award signed by two of three (two appraisers or one plus the umpire) is generally binding.
Texas licenses adjusters through TDI; appraisers must be competent and independent under the policy.
body_html:
The core difference in an insurance appraiser vs adjuster comparison is the job each one does. An adjuster investigates the claim, interprets coverage, and proposes a payment. An insurance appraiser steps in only when you and the insurer disagree on the amount of loss, and determines what the covered damage is actually worth.

Both roles show up in Texas property claims, both inspect damage, and both write estimates. That overlap is why so many homeowners mix them up. But who they work for, what authority they hold, and when they enter your claim are very different. Knowing which professional you need at each stage can save you months of frustration and thousands of dollars on a hail, wind, water, or fire claim.

What Is an Insurance Adjuster?

An insurance adjuster is usually the first professional you deal with after you report a loss. The adjuster inspects the property, photographs the damage, reviews your policy, and prepares an estimate that becomes the carrier's settlement offer.

Adjusters handle the full life of a claim. They decide whether a loss is covered, what caused it, which exclusions apply, and what the policy owes after depreciation and your deductible. In other words, the adjuster answers two questions at once: Is this covered? and How much is it worth?

The three types of adjusters in Texas

  • Staff (company) adjusters are employees of the insurance company and work only on its claims.
  • Independent adjusters are contractors hired by insurers, often in large numbers after a major Texas hailstorm or hurricane. They still represent the insurer.
  • Public adjusters are licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance to represent policyholders. They help prepare, document, and negotiate the claim on your behalf, usually for a percentage of the settlement.

Staff and independent adjusters both work for the carrier. That does not make them dishonest, but it does mean their estimates follow the carrier's guidelines, pricing choices, and scope decisions.

What Is an Insurance Appraiser?

An insurance appraiser (sometimes called an insurance claims appraiser or property damage appraiser) is a professional appointed under the appraisal clause of your policy. Most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies include this clause. It lets either side demand appraisal when both agree a loss is covered but cannot agree on the amount of loss.

Once appraisal is invoked, you choose your appraiser and the insurer chooses its appraiser. The two appraisers inspect the property, compare line-item estimates, and try to agree on a number. If they cannot, an umpire resolves the remaining items. An award signed by any two of the three is generally binding on the amount of loss. You can read a full walkthrough in our guide to what an insurance appraisal is.

An appraiser does not decide coverage. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), the Texas Supreme Court held that appraisers determine the amount of loss and may assess causation and the extent of damage, but questions of coverage and liability remain for the insurer and, ultimately, the courts.

What does "independent insurance appraiser" mean?

Most appraisal clauses require each side's appraiser to be "competent and disinterested" or "independent." In practice, that means your appraiser should have no financial stake in the outcome beyond a reasonable fee, and should not be your contractor or someone who will profit from the repair. An independent insurance appraiser brings estimating expertise to your side of the table while still meeting the policy's impartiality standard.

Appraiser vs Adjuster: Key Differences at a Glance

The table below summarizes how the two roles compare on a typical Texas property claim.

FactorInsurance AdjusterInsurance Appraiser
When involvedFrom the first notice of lossOnly after a dispute over the amount of loss and a written appraisal demand
Who they representThe insurer (staff or independent) or the policyholder (public adjuster)The side that appointed them, under a duty of impartiality set by the policy
Decides coverage?Yes (carrier adjusters make coverage recommendations)No, coverage and liability stay outside appraisal
Decides amount of loss?Proposes an amount the insurer can reviseSets a binding amount with the other appraiser or umpire
Texas licenseRequired (TDI adjuster license)No specific appraiser license; competence and independence required by the policy
Typical work productInspection report, estimate, coverage letterLine-item estimate, negotiation with opposing appraiser, signed appraisal award
How paidSalary or carrier fee; public adjusters take a percentageEach side pays its own appraiser and splits the umpire, per most policies

Who Does an Adjuster or Appraiser Work For?

The adjuster vs appraiser question often comes down to loyalty. A carrier adjuster is paid by the company that pays your claim. Their estimate reflects the insurer's software settings, pricing assumptions, and internal review. Many are fair and thorough, but they are working through a large caseload, sometimes hundreds of claims after a single storm.

A public adjuster works for you from the start, negotiating with the carrier. Still, a public adjuster can only negotiate. If the insurer refuses to move, the public adjuster cannot force a number.

An appraiser is different because appraisal is a binding process. Your appraiser builds the strongest accurate estimate of your loss and negotiates with the insurer's appraiser. If the two cannot agree, the umpire decides. That structure is what gives appraisal its teeth.

Tip: Hiring a policyholder-side appraiser does not mean you were wrong to work with the adjuster first. Appraisal usually comes after the adjuster's estimate, once it is clear the gap will not close through normal negotiation.

Scope of Authority: Coverage vs Amount of Loss

This is the single most important distinction between an insurance appraiser and an adjuster.

Adjusters can:

  • Interpret policy language, exclusions, and endorsements
  • Decide (or recommend) whether a loss is covered
  • Investigate cause of loss and timing
  • Apply depreciation, deductibles, and limits
  • Propose and revise settlement amounts

Appraisers can:

  • Inspect the damage and measure the property
  • Determine what it costs to repair or replace covered damage
  • Evaluate whether specific damage resulted from the claimed event, when the dispute is over the extent of storm damage
  • Resolve pricing, scope, and quantity disputes line by line
  • Sign a binding appraisal award on the amount of loss

Because appraisal is limited to amount of loss, it works best when the insurer agrees there is covered damage but pays too little: underscoped roofs, missing line items, low unit prices, or refused matching. Pure coverage denials usually need a different approach, although our article on whether you can invoke appraisal after a denied claim explains the gray areas.

Insurance Producer vs Adjuster vs Appraiser

A third role adds to the confusion: the insurance producer. In Texas, "producer" is the licensing term for an agent who sells policies. Your agent helps you buy coverage and may help you report a claim, but they do not adjust the claim or set its value.

  • Producer (agent): sells and services the policy.
  • Adjuster: investigates and values the claim.
  • Appraiser: resolves a disagreement over the amount of loss through the appraisal clause.

If your agent tells you the adjuster's number is final, remember that the policy itself usually gives you the appraisal option.

When Should You Hire an Insurance Appraiser Instead of Relying on the Adjuster?

Consider appraisal when the adjuster agrees the loss is covered but the payment is far from what repairs will cost. Common warning signs include:

  • The carrier pays for a roof repair while your contractor says the roof needs full replacement.
  • Line items such as drip edge, starter, flashing, or code upgrades are missing.
  • Unit prices are far below what Texas contractors actually charge.
  • The insurer refuses to pay to match siding, flooring, or shingles.
  • Supplements and re-inspections have stalled with no movement.

Our guide to the signs your insurance claim was underpaid walks through these red flags in more detail. Before deciding, run your numbers through the appraisal cost calculator to see whether the potential recovery justifies the cost.

How Adjusting and Appraisal Work in Texas

Texas sees some of the most frequent hail and wind losses in the country, from the DFW Metroplex to Central Texas and the Gulf Coast. That volume puts heavy pressure on adjusters after big storms, which is one reason appraisal is used so often here.

A few Texas-specific points matter:

  • Adjuster licensing. Adjusters, including public adjusters, are licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance.
  • Prompt payment deadlines. Under Texas Insurance Code chapter 542, insurers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days and accept or reject it within 15 business days after receiving requested information, with limited extensions.
  • Appraisal and later claims. In Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), the court held that paying an appraisal award does not automatically bar a prompt-payment claim. This is general information, not legal advice; talk to a Texas attorney about your specific rights.

Our Texas claim deadline calculator can help you track the key dates on your claim.

Can One Professional Be Both an Adjuster and an Appraiser?

Yes, the skills overlap. Joseph Dittman, the appraiser behind TX Insurance Appraiser, is a Texas-licensed public adjuster who has spent his career on the policyholder side: inspecting storm, water, and fire losses, writing Xactimate and Symbility estimates, and negotiating with carrier adjusters. That background is what makes an effective appraiser.

The roles stay separate on a given claim, though. When Joseph is appointed as your appraiser (or as umpire), he serves in that role only, not as your public adjuster or attorney on that claim. That separation keeps the appraisal compliant with the policy's independence requirements.

Next Steps if the Adjuster's Number Is Too Low

  1. Get the adjuster's full estimate in writing, line by line.
  2. Document everything with photos, measurements, and contractor estimates. Our claim documentation checklist helps.
  3. Compare scope and pricing to identify the real gap.
  4. Read your policy's appraisal clause for the demand procedure and deadlines.
  5. Talk to an experienced appraiser before sending a written demand.

faqs.q: Is an insurance appraiser the same as an insurance adjuster?
faqs.a: No. An adjuster investigates a claim, interprets coverage, and proposes a settlement, usually on behalf of the insurer. An insurance appraiser is appointed under the policy's appraisal clause only when both sides disagree on the amount of loss. The appraiser values the covered damage and, with the other appraiser or umpire, signs a binding award.

faqs.q: Who pays for an insurance appraiser?
faqs.a: Under most Texas appraisal clauses, each side pays its own appraiser, and the policyholder and insurer split the umpire's fee equally if an umpire is needed. Appraiser fees vary by claim size and complexity, so compare the expected cost against the gap between the carrier's estimate and the realistic repair cost before invoking appraisal.

faqs.q: Does an insurance appraiser need a license in Texas?
faqs.a: Texas does not issue a specific license for insurance appraisers in property appraisal. Instead, most policies require each appraiser to be competent and disinterested or independent. Adjusters, including public adjusters, must be licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance. Many effective appraisers have adjusting or estimating backgrounds and write detailed Xactimate or Symbility estimates.

faqs.q: Can my contractor act as my insurance appraiser?
faqs.a: Usually not. Because most appraisal clauses require an independent or disinterested appraiser, a contractor who expects to perform the repairs has a financial interest in the outcome. Using them as your appraiser invites a challenge to the award. Contractors can still supply estimates, photos, and repair input to your appraiser as supporting evidence.

faqs.q: Should I hire a public adjuster or an appraiser?
faqs.a: A public adjuster helps you build and negotiate the claim from the start. An appraiser is the better fit once the insurer accepts coverage but you remain far apart on price or scope and negotiation has stalled. Appraisal produces a binding number, while negotiation depends on the insurer agreeing to move.
